extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of philosophy/logic (readers studying the theory of propositions, predication, and classification)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing the import and types of propositions, the distinction between verbal (essential) and real (accidental) propositions, and the logical principles governing classification and predication (the five predicables).

rubrics_metrics.name: Five kinds of matters-of-fact asserted in propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence, Co-existence, Sequence (Order in Time), Causation, Resemblance are the exhaustive five things asserted (or denied) in every non-verbal proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly states that 'Existence, Co-existence, Sequence, Causation, Resemblance: one or other of these is asserted (or denied) in every proposition which is not merely verbal.' Use this five-fold division as an exhaustive classification when analyzing what a proposition actually asserts. Example uses and transformations (into concrete terms) are provided throughout the chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Order in Place (spatial order) from Co-inherence/Order in Time
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions of Co-existence come in two kinds: propositions of Order in Place (accounting for place) and propositions of Co-inherence of Attributes (concurrence of attributes or powers in the same part/locality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that co-inherence (attributes co-existing within the same object or the same part) is different from spatial Order in Place. The text exemplifies co-inherence (e.g., properties of gold or functions of mind) and notes that co-inherence belongs to simultaneity and therefore to Time rather than Place. Treat co-inherence as a complex case of temporal co-existence (sometimes potential rather than actual).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract propositions can be transformed into concrete equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Any proposition expressed in abstract terms can be converted into a precisely equivalent proposition using concrete terms either naming the attributes themselves or the fundamenta (facts/phenomena) grounding those attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing abstract-term propositions, reformulate them into concrete propositions to expose the underlying matter-of-fact (existence, sequence, causation, co-existence, or resemblance). Examples: 'Thoughtlessness is dangerous' → 'Thoughtless actions are dangerous.' 'Whiteness is a color' → 'The sensation of sight caused by looking at snow is one of the sensations called sensations of white.' This transformability is presented as a general method of analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential (merely verbal) vs Accidental (real) propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Essential propositions assert only what is implied by the meaning of a name (purely verbal) and therefore are not strictly susceptible of truth/falsity except as conformity to usage; Accidental (non-essential or Real) propositions predicate attributes not connoted by the subject and thus convey information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to judge whether a proposition adds factual information. Essential propositions often only unfold the meaning of a term (and may tacitly imply existence because of copula ambiguity). Accidental propositions (including propositions about individuals or where predicate adds new connotation) are the ones that legitimately inform and can serve as premises in reasoning. Avoid treating essential propositions as substantive logical examples because they can mislead about the utility of syllogistic reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions as the most useful essential propositions (completeness criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions are a kind of essential proposition which should, to be complete, 'unfold the whole of what is involved in the meaning of the word defined' (i.e., the whole of what it connotes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good (complete) definition should specify the entire connotation of a connotative term, though in practice we often give only enough connotation to distinguish the denoted objects from others. The author notes that sometimes an accidental property suffices for distinguishing a class; different kinds of definition serve different purposes and will be considered later.

rubrics_metrics.name: A proposition's practical import: propositions as marks/evidence for use in reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: When considered as memoranda for practical use, a general proposition (e.g., 'All men are mortal') functions as indicating that the attributes of the subject are evidence or a mark of the predicate (i.e., they are signs by which the presence of the predicate is made manifest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For reasoning (where propositions serve as means to establish other propositions), prefer the formulation that presents a proposition as asserting 'one fact is a mark or evidence of another.' This practical view highlights how propositions are to be used in advancing from premises to conclusions and is 'almost indispensable' in the theory of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicables: fivefold classification of predicate relations
rubrics_metrics.description: The five predicables are genus, species, differentia, proprium, and accidens. These distinctions classify the kind of class-name the predicate denotes relative to the subject, not what the predicate means in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying a predicate in a given proposition, determine the relation it bears to the subject: e.g., 'animal' is a genus with respect to man but a species with respect to 'substance.' The same name can serve different predicables depending on the subject. Use these categories to analyze classification and predication in logical arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: General names create classes by connotation; classification depends on connotative attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: A general name that connotes attributes constitutes a class ipso facto of the things possessing those attributes; classes often owe their existence to general language, though sometimes names are introduced to create useful classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analyzing classification, treat general names as signifying attributes rather than presupposing pre-existing natural classes. Whether a name is introduced because of existing common attributes or for convenience in forming a class, its signification remains an expression of those attributes (e.g., Cuvier's class names express attributes). The principles that should govern classification as a logical process are deferred to later chapters, but this passage emphasizes that connotation, not a metaphysical universal-substance, underlies class formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: avoid using essential propositions as main examples in teaching logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Using essential propositions (those that only unfold the meaning of names) as the principal examples in logic instruction is misleading, because they add no information beyond the meanings of the words and thereby make syllogistic reasoning appear useless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes historical misuse where school logic illustrated predication and syllogism almost exclusively with essential propositions (e.g., 'All men are rational'), which gives the false impression that syllogistic art is of little use. As a pedagogical rule, favor examples where predicates add factual content (accidental propositions) when demonstrating logical inference.
